claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed surface oxide layer.
At room temperature, the natural oxide layer suppresses corrosion by passivating the Q235 steel surface.
At elevated temperature, the natural oxide layer undergoes a phase transformation.
The elevated-temperature phase transformation produces micro-cracks in the oxide layer.
Micro-cracks in the transformed oxide promote localized corrosion in chloride-containing environments.
At room temperature, the intact oxide remains stable and limits the formation of active corrosion sites.
The elevated-temperature oxide phase has reduced protective properties.
Defects in the transformed oxide act as localized-corrosion initiation sites through galvanic interactions.
At approximately 25°C, naturally oxidized Q235 steel will have a lower corrosion rate than oxide-removed Q235 steel.
At approximately 80°C, Q235 steel with the intact natural oxide will have a significantly higher corrosion rate than oxide-removed Q235 steel.
The proposed temperature-dependent corrosion behavior is governed by structural and phase changes in the natural oxide layer.
